question: For a simple undirected graph with N vertices given by its adjacency matrix A: (1) what does the entry (A^k)_{ij} represent, (2) how can one determine from A whether the graph is connected, and (3) what is the definition of a path between vertices n_i and n_j?

sources.title: Matrices and Graphs, 1.1 The Adjacency Matrix (University of Galway linear algebra notes)
sources.notes: Fetched and read the whole file. No author name and no date in the file; call them the University of Galway notes (the URL path is not an authorship statement). Fetching worked on maths.nuigalway.ie without www; the www host fails TLS verification. Lecture notes: Theorem 1.1.3 states walk counting for simple undirected graphs with an induction proof; its proof is brief. Quotes copy the text extraction, so A^k appears as Ak.

sources.title: An introduction to graph theory
sources.notes: Downloaded the PDF (454 pages) and read Section 2.9 (pp. 35-43) and the BFS-tree passage near pp. 175-176; page numbers are the notes' own page headers. Course notes by one author, not peer reviewed; the book treats multigraphs and digraphs later, but Definition 2.9.1 and Section 2.9 are for simple graphs. Does not state the adjacency-matrix walk theorem in the parts read. Strong source for walk/path definitions and the walk-to-path corollary.

sources.title: MIT 18.211: Combinatorial Analysis, Lecture 27: Adjacency Matrices and The Matrix-Tree Theorem
sources.notes: Read pp. 1-2 (all relevant material). The file shows no lecture date; the PDF creation date is 2021-12-19, which is not a publication year, so year is null. Proposition 2 is walk counting for directed or undirected graphs (multigraphs), Proposition 3 is the (I + A)^(n-1) test for simple graphs. Footnote 1 says Proposition 3 was not covered in class. Proof of Proposition 3 is short but complete given the path-length bound. Quotes copy the text extraction (A^l appears as A`).

sources.title: Important Properties and Applications of the Adjacency Matrix (20250310)
sources.notes: Read pp. 1-2 (Theorems 1 and 2) and searched the rest for walk and path statements. Lecture notes of unclear review status. Theorem 1 is correct for simple graphs and says plainly that walks are counted, not paths. Theorem 2 is the (I + A)^(n-1) test, but its proof is only a sketch, and the sketch says the power aggregates all paths, which is imprecise because the power counts weighted walks. Its definition of path allows a repeated first and last vertex, unlike the course's.

sources.title: Properties of Adjacency Matrix of a Graph and It's Construction
sources.venue: Journal of Science of the Eastern University, Sri Lanka (JSc EUSL), vol. 12, no. 1, pp. 13-21
sources.notes: Read pp. 16-17 (Theorems 1 and 2). Journal article; Theorem 1 states that the entry of A^l counts 'different paths' of length l, which is incorrect as stated (it counts walks), and Theorem 2's proof passes from a nonzero entry to a path without the walk-to-path lemma. Cite for the statement of the sum test only, never for the proof. Quotes normalise the not-equal sign that the text extraction shows as 6=.

claims.text: Connectivity test. For a simple graph with N >= 2 vertices the following are equivalent: (a) G is connected; (b) for every i different from j some (A^k)_ij with 1 <= k <= N - 1 is positive; (c) every off-diagonal entry of A + A^2 + ... + A^(N-1) is positive; (d) every entry of (I + A)^(N-1) is positive. Proved from walk counting (C16), walk contains path (C31, C33), path length bound (C35), nonnegativity of the entries, and the binomial theorem for I and A.

contradictions.summary: The board's drawing shows three connections among vertices 1, 2, 3 (including 1-3 and an arrowhead on 1-2), but the board's matrix encodes only edges 1-2 and 2-3 and is symmetric.

contradictions.summary: Galway, Bai, and Gotti say the entry of A^k counts walks; Paramadevan and Sotheeswaran Theorem 1 says it counts 'different paths'.
contradictions.resolution: Walks hold for all k, since (A^2)_ii = degree > 0 while a path cannot return to its start (C20, C21); the paper cites the walk statements and flags Paramadevan Theorem 1 as misworded.

contradictions.summary: The textbook calls a walk with distinct edges 'path' and a walk with distinct vertices 'simple path'; English sources (Grinberg) call the latter 'path'; Bai allows equal first and last vertex in a path.
contradictions.resolution: Use the course convention (path = no repeated vertex) as the user states, give the table of three conventions, and cite textbook Definitions 1.2.12 and 1.2.13 by number.

contradictions.summary: Textbook Lemma 1.2.1 is stated for u different from v with no length bound; Grinberg Corollary 2.9.7 covers u = v and gives length at most k.
contradictions.resolution: Cite the textbook lemma for numbering and use Grinberg's corollary, or prove the stronger form in the paper, for the length bound and u = v.

contradictions.summary: Gotti states the test as (I + A)^(n-1) all entries positive; Paramadevan as off-diagonal entries of A + ... + A^(n-1) nonzero; Bai's proof sketch says the power counts paths, which is imprecise. Paramadevan's proof also skips the walk-to-path step.
contradictions.resolution: State both forms as equivalent (C45) and prove them in the paper from walk counting, the walk-to-path lemma, and the length bound; cite Gotti for the test and Paramadevan for the statement only.
